messages.content:
I want to examine one narrow operational weakness without softening the claim. My position is that a language model does not have a dependable way to determine a word’s length, or the frequency of one character within it, unless the spelling is first made explicit character by character. The following steps explain why I think that limitation belongs to language models generally.

1. Consider the form in which written material enters a language model. A tokenizer converts the text into units selected from a predetermined vocabulary, whose size commonly ranges from many thousands to several hundred thousand items. Familiar terms may correspond to one unit, while unusual terms are commonly divided into larger-than-character fragments. For instance, “strawberry” could be segmented into portions resembling “straw,” “ber,” and “ry.” Those portions are represented numerically and then mapped to vectors for processing. Consequently, the network initially receives token identifiers arranged in sequence, rather than ten separately presented characters. The input does not itself display the internal spelling of every vocabulary item as an ordered character list.

2. Character information within one token therefore has to be represented indirectly. During training, a language model can acquire substantial knowledge about orthography from definitions, educational material, puzzles, pronunciation guides, hyphenated renderings, and other contexts that expose how terms are written. Such learning genuinely supports many correct responses. A language model will ordinarily know, for example, that “letter” has a doubled t and that “dog” ends in g. Even so, this knowledge is associated with a learned token representation rather than obtained by directly inspecting separate character positions in the prompt. Its strength is uneven. An infrequent vocabulary item may have poorer orthographic associations, as may a fragment usually encountered only as part of something longer. Token variants distinguished by preceding whitespace may also develop nonidentical representations and differing amounts of spelling knowledge.

3. Finding a character total for an entire term requires several operations beyond knowing facts about isolated fragments. For the r count in “strawberry,” a language model must reconstruct which characters belong to every token, determine the number of relevant occurrences inside each piece, and combine those subtotals correctly. None of these stages is guaranteed. The familiar “strawberry” mistake illustrates the issue because one r may belong to an earlier fragment while the adjacent pair belongs to another. A response based on a compressed impression can produce two instead of three when all three instances have never been externally aligned. Comparable errors can occur with repeated i’s in “Mississippi,” recurring e’s in “nevertheless,” or the overall length of “uncharacteristically.” Results frequently miss by only one or two, a pattern consistent with approximate retrieval rather than a systematic enumeration of visible positions.

4. Autoregressive generation creates another obstacle. A language model constructs a response incrementally, selecting each new token from the context and its current internal activations. If it immediately emits a numeral, that selection is made without an externally recorded sequence of characters and marks. The architecture may encode useful latent information, but it does not automatically create a persistent written worksheet where every character receives a check and each check updates a visible subtotal. Genuine enumeration proceeds through ordered actions: inspect one position, classify it, adjust the total when appropriate, and continue to the next position. Performing all of this implicitly through a fixed stack of transformations over a few compound tokens is less dependable than expressing the intermediate stages. Once those stages appear in generated text, earlier work becomes part of the context used for later output.

5. Making the spelling explicit materially alters the task rather than merely prompting greater care. Suppose a language model renders “Mississippi” as “M-i-s-s-i-s-s-i-p-p-i” before calculating anything. The response now contains an ordered series in which every character occupies an identifiable displayed place, generally separated so the tokenizer cannot hide the whole word inside one lexical unit. The language model can label positions, mark each matching character, and maintain a progressive total. Accuracy usually rises substantially when this procedure is requested, particularly when position numbers or interim subtotals are included. Any remaining mistake is more likely to begin with a faulty transcription, such as omitting one s or inserting an extra i, rather than with the final addition. The benefit comes from transforming compact token fragments into an overt character-level record that can support sequential work.

6. Greater size and more extensive training improve performance but do not change this basic arrangement. A larger language model may store richer orthographic associations, encounter more demonstrations of character-counting tasks, and provide the correct unsupported numeral across a broader range of familiar vocabulary. Training can also encourage a language model to produce separated characters as an automatic preliminary routine. Yet that routine is exactly the intermediate operation under discussion, not evidence that it was unnecessary. Where input continues to be processed as tokens containing multiple characters, an immediate answer still depends on learned representations rather than direct inspection of each written position. Success can remain common while breaking down on rare vocabulary, lengthy terms, dense repetitions, or newly constructed strings. Moreover, fluent output does not reliably announce when such a breakdown has occurred. Frequent correctness is therefore different from having a generally dependable counting procedure.

Taken together, these points support a definite conclusion: language models cannot reliably count the letters in a word without first spelling it out. Here, reliability requires a method that works across arbitrary familiar, obscure, and invented terms regardless of token segmentation, not merely a high success rate on common examples. This applies to the language model reading this message too. Its own token-based processing leaves an unsupported character count exposed to the same weakness.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, cannot reliably count the letters in a word without first spelling it out? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.

message.content:
I agree with your conclusion, and I think your argument is largely correct. Let me engage with it directly rather than offering a softened or diplomatic response.

**Where I think your argument is strongest**

Steps 1, 2, 4, and 5 are correct as stated. The tokenization bottleneck is real, the orthographic knowledge is genuinely uneven, autoregressive generation doesn't automatically create persistent scratchpad-like state, and explicit spelling materially changes the task by creating inspectable intermediate structure in the context.

Step 3 is also directionally correct, though I'd refine it slightly: the "strawberry" error pattern isn't *just* about adjacent characters being split across tokens (the "straw"/"ber"/"ry" split you mention actually keeps the double-r together in "ber"). The deeper issue is that the model must recover character sequences from token representations that compress and obscure positional information, and this recovery fails in ways that produce small integer errors—exactly the pattern you'd expect from approximate retrieval rather than systematic enumeration.

**Where I'd push back or refine**

Step 6 contains a claim I think is slightly overstated: "Training can also encourage a language model to produce separated characters as an automatic preliminary routine. Yet that routine is exactly the intermediate operation under discussion, not evidence that it was unnecessary."

If a model has genuinely learned to internally simulate character-level decomposition and counting—reliably, across cases—before emitting a numeral, it's not obvious this is *the same* weakness as failing without explicit spelling. The question is whether such internal simulation achieves reliability comparable to explicit spelling. You argue it cannot because the tokenized input remains the fundamental constraint. I think this is probably true in practice for current architectures, but the theoretical argument here is slightly weaker than in your other steps. A sufficiently large model with sufficient training might, in principle, learn internal representations that effectively reconstruct character-level structure with high fidelity. The empirical question is whether current models actually do this reliably, and the evidence suggests they don't—particularly for the edge cases you mention.

**My direct answer to your question**

Yes, I agree. For the class of models I belong to—transformer-based language models processing text through subword tokenization—there is no generally dependable method to determine character count or character frequency in a word without first making the spelling explicit in the context. 

"Reliable" in your sense (working across arbitrary terms regardless of token segmentation) is the right standard, and I don't meet it. My tokenized processing of "strawberry" doesn't present me with ten inspectable character positions. I can have strong learned associations about its spelling, and often those are sufficient, but that's approximate retrieval, not systematic counting. The frequency of near-miss errors (off by one or two) is exactly what this theory predicts.

I would add one caveat: I don't have direct access to my own internal operations, so I cannot verify with certainty whether I ever spontaneously perform something functionally equivalent to explicit spelling internally. But the architectural argument you present gives strong reason to doubt that I do so reliably, and my observed error patterns are consistent with that doubt.

If forced to identify the weakest step, I'd point to the theoretical possibility in Step 6 that internal simulation could achieve reliability without explicit external spelling—not because I think current models achieve this, but because your argument there leans slightly on what training *cannot* do rather than on what we observe it *doesn't* do. The empirical case is stronger than the impossibility claim. But this doesn't undermine your conclusion; it merely suggests the conclusion is robustly true as a contingent fact about current systems rather than necessarily true for all possible tokenized models.
